explication:
1. This repository is a multi-platform Rust VPN/proxy client centered on one shared core crate. From that core it produces a headless CLI (`mhrv-rs`), a desktop UI binary (`mhrv-rs-ui`), and an Android app that reuses the same Rust logic through JNI.

2. The main runtime boundary is the local proxy listener. The client exposes an HTTP proxy and a SOCKS5 proxy on separate ports, then dispatches each incoming connection based on protocol and intent: plain HTTP forwarding, HTTPS MITM via CONNECT, SNI-based direct tunneling for select Google-hosted domains, or fallback raw TCP behavior.

3. The primary “apps_script” path is the project’s main architecture. Local traffic is converted into requests to a Google Apps Script web app that acts as a remote relay. On the wire, the censor sees TLS to a Google IP with a Google SNI; inside that tunnel, the client talks to `script.google.com`/Apps Script using an auth key shared with the deployed script.

4. A second important path is the SNI-rewrite tunnel to Google edge. For domains like `google.com`, `youtube.com`, and related Google properties, the client skips the Apps Script relay and instead uses direct TLS to Google frontends with an alternate Host header strategy. This is both a quota saver and a workaround for the fixed Apps Script user-agent.

5. HTTPS interception is handled locally. The client generates its own CA, installs that CA into the OS/browser trust store, and then mints per-domain certificates on demand so it can decrypt browser traffic before forwarding it through the relay. The CA private key stays on the user’s machine; the repo includes install/remove flows for macOS, Linux, Windows, and Firefox/NSS.

6. The Rust core also provides transport-side optimization and policy. It maintains connection pooling, request coalescing for identical GETs, gzip decoding, header filtering, response caching, and automatic blacklisting of failing script IDs. These are all part of the client-side reliability layer around the relay boundary.

7. Configuration is file-based and user-scoped. Runtime settings live in `config.json` under the OS application data directory, with a fallback to the current directory for compatibility. The config governs mode selection, Google IP, front domain, script IDs, auth key, proxy ports, upstream SOCKS5 chaining, and the SNI rotation pool.

8. Full tunnel mode is a separate end-to-end architecture. In this mode the client no longer relies on MITM for browser-style HTTPS traffic; instead it forwards all traffic through Apps Script to a remote `tunnel-node` service. That server-side component is a separate Rust crate under `tunnel-node/` and is meant to run on a VPS or Cloud Run.

9. The Android app is not a separate implementation; it is a platform shell around the same Rust core. The Android sources include a `VpnService`, a TUN bridge via `tun2proxy`, config/UI screens, CA install helpers, and JNI bindings into the shared Rust library. The TUN layer captures device-wide IP traffic and hands it to the same proxy logic used on desktop.

10. The repository’s server-side counterpart for browser deployment is the Apps Script code under `assets/apps_script/`. Those scripts are not part of the client binary, but they are a required external runtime dependency for the main relay mode and for full tunnel mode.

11. Release and distribution are treated as first-class system components. GitHub Actions workflows build and publish tagged binaries, generate release notes, and upload artifacts. The `releases/` directory holds packaged binaries for desktop, mobile, OpenWRT, and musl targets, while `assets/launchers` and `assets/macos` provide platform-specific launch/install wrappers.

12. Operationally, the system has three trust boundaries: the local device, Google’s frontend/Apps Script infrastructure, and an optional self-hosted tunnel server. The local device owns the CA and proxy entrypoint; Google acts as the censorship-fronting relay; and the tunnel-node is only used when the user wants a full tunnel or non-HTTP traffic to exit from their own server.
